items.q: Describe the economy of the Harappan civilisation.
items.proposedAnswer: The economy rested on agriculture, with crops such as wheat and barley, and on crafts such as bead making and pottery. Trade, including with distant regions, linked it to other societies.

items.q: Why was a drainage system important in a densely populated Harappan city?
items.proposedAnswer: A drainage system carried waste water away, keeping streets and homes clean and lowering the risk of disease. Its planning also shows that the city had some organised civic arrangements.

items.q: Name any two Gupta rulers.
items.proposedAnswer: Chandragupta I and Samudragupta were Gupta rulers. Chandragupta II and Skandagupta are others.

items.q: What role did guilds play in the economy of ancient India?
items.proposedAnswer: Guilds organised crafts and trade, set standards and rules for members, and some also took deposits and lent money. Many guilds also supported religious institutions through donations.

items.q: Mention two teachings of Kabir.
items.proposedAnswer: Kabir taught devotion to one formless God and criticised idol worship and empty ritual. He also rejected caste distinctions and urged simple, honest living.

items.q: How did the Mughal state try to win the loyalty of regional elites?
items.proposedAnswer: It gave ranks and offices to nobles of different backgrounds, including Rajput chiefs, and formed marriage alliances with some ruling families. A policy of religious tolerance and recognition of local zamindars also helped.

items.q: Name two social reforms of the nineteenth century linked to reformers or the government.
items.proposedAnswer: The practice of sati was banned in 1829 during William Bentinck's time, with the support of reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy. The Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 followed efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

items.q: Evaluate the effects of the railways on India's economy under British rule.
items.proposedAnswer: Railways joined markets and moved raw materials to ports, helping trade and also famine relief. However, they mainly served British commercial and military needs, and much of the benefit went to Britain.
keyPoints: Helped movement of goods and relief

items.q: Mention two constructive programmes promoted by Gandhi.
items.proposedAnswer: Gandhi promoted khadi and spinning to encourage self-reliance. He also worked for the removal of untouchability and for harmony among communities.

items.q: How did newspapers in Indian languages help spread nationalist ideas?
items.proposedAnswer: They carried news and criticism of British policies to people who did not read English. They helped create public opinion, which is why the government tried to control them, as in the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

items.q: What does the word sovereign in the Preamble mean?
items.proposedAnswer: Sovereign means that India is fully independent and has supreme authority over its own affairs. It is not subject to the control of any outside power.

items.q: Why was it significant that the Constitution was drafted by a Constituent Assembly of Indians and not by the British Parliament?
items.proposedAnswer: It meant that Indians themselves framed the rules of their government, which gave the Constitution legitimacy. The members, chosen mainly by the provincial assemblies, represented many regions and views.

items.q: State two functions of the Election Commission of India.
items.proposedAnswer: The Election Commission conducts free and fair elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. It also prepares electoral rolls and enforces the Model Code of Conduct.

items.q: How do the legislature, executive and judiciary act as checks on one another?
items.proposedAnswer: The legislature makes laws and holds the executive accountable through questions and votes. The executive carries out laws and can be questioned in courts, while the judiciary can strike down laws or actions that violate the Constitution.
keyPoints: Legislature makes laws and holds the executive accountable

items.q: What was the Berlin Wall and what did its fall in 1989 symbolise?
items.proposedAnswer: The Berlin Wall divided East and West Berlin from 1961. Its fall in 1989 symbolised the end of the division of Europe and the approaching end of the Cold War.
keyPoints: Symbol of the end of Cold War divisions

items.q: How did the formation of the European Union reflect the idea of integration after the Second World War?
items.proposedAnswer: After the destruction of the war, European countries sought to prevent future conflict through economic cooperation, beginning with joint control of coal and steel in the early 1950s. This grew into a common market and later the Union with shared institutions.

items.q: Describe two characteristics of rural settlements.
items.proposedAnswer: Most people in rural settlements depend on agriculture and related primary activities. Settlements are usually small, with fewer services, and are closely tied to land and local resources.

items.q: Why do young people from some rural regions move to cities?
items.proposedAnswer: Rural areas may offer few jobs outside farming and limited schools and health services. Cities offer wider employment and better facilities, so these push and pull factors lead to migration.
keyPoints: Better jobs and services in cities

items.proposedAnswer: Renewable resources, such as solar energy or wind, are replenished naturally and are not exhausted by use. Non-renewable resources, such as coal or petroleum, take millions of years to form and can be used up.

items.q: How does agriculture contribute to industrial development?
items.proposedAnswer: Agriculture supplies raw materials such as cotton, jute and sugarcane to industries. It also provides a market for industrial goods such as fertilisers and machinery and gives employment to many people.
